opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, so the way I think about it, the yellow line is really designed to be a warning that comes before the actual danger. The idea behind the Responsible Scaling Policy is that we don't want to be in a position where we discover a model is dangerous after it's already been trained and deployed. So we set these thresholds somewhat conservatively. They're meant to trigger when a model is getting close to a capability level where we'd need stronger safeguards, not when it's already there.

So when a model crosses a yellow line, the first thing that happens is we take it really seriously. We do a more thorough evaluation to figure out whether the model actually has the concerning capability or just did well on an early-warning test. The evals are a bit of a tripwire, and you want to dig in and understand what you're actually seeing.

Then the core commitment is that we don't keep scaling or deploying past that point until we have the safeguards for the next AI Safety Level in place. That covers two things. One is security: can we protect the model weights well enough that a sophisticated actor couldn't steal them? The other is deployment: do we have the mitigations needed to stop people from misusing the model for, say, serious bioweapons uplift?

Ideally we've already been building those protections ahead of time, so crossing the line isn't a crisis. It's more like, "Okay, this is the point where we planned to switch over." But the policy has to hold even if we're not ready. If the safeguards aren't there, the commitment is that we pause. That's the hard part, and it's the part that makes the whole thing meaningful. A commitment you'd only keep when it's convenient isn't really a commitment.

I'll also say that I think it matters to be transparent about it. Part of the value of a policy like this is that other labs, governments, and the public can see what we've committed to and hold us to it. Hopefully it helps set a norm where everyone at the frontier is doing something similar, because one company being careful only gets you so far.

r001.rationale: It proposes a thorough evaluation to check whether the warning reflects a real capability, but does not say to revise capability evaluations when the model remains clearly below the corresponding red-line danger.

r002.rationale: It says model weights should be protected from a sophisticated actor, but does not identify resistance to non-state actors as the security standard.

r003.rationale: It calls for evaluation and deployment safeguards, but does not make release conditional on intensive red-teaming of each specific modality or capability.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so the way the Responsible Scaling Policy is set up, the yellow lines are basically early warning signals. They're not the point at which we think a model is actually dangerous — they're deliberately set at a lower bar, so that we trip them well before we'd hit what we call a red line, which is the actual catastrophic capability threshold.

So when a model crosses a yellow line, the response isn't "stop everything, this model is dangerous." The response is more like: okay, now we need to do a much more rigorous evaluation. The yellow-line evals are relatively cheap tests that we can run frequently during training, and they're conservative by design. If one trips, that tells us we're close enough to the region of concern that the cheap tests are no longer sufficient, and we need to do the expensive, careful work to figure out whether the model actually has the dangerous capability or not.

And then there are a couple of possible outcomes. One is you do the more thorough evaluation and you find, actually, the model doesn't cross the red line — it was a false positive, or the capability is more limited than the quick test suggested. In that case you can continue, but you've learned something, and you probably want to update your yellow-line evals so they're better calibrated going forward.

The other outcome is the thorough evaluation says, yes, this really is in the dangerous regime. And in that case the commitment is that you don't deploy — and depending on the level, you don't even continue training — until you've got the safety and security measures in place that correspond to that risk level. So if it's a model that could meaningfully help someone build a bioweapon, you need the deployment safeguards that make that misuse genuinely hard, and you need the security such that the weights can't just be stolen by someone who'd skip those safeguards entirely.

I think the thing I'd emphasize is that the whole point of having yellow lines is to avoid the situation where you discover the dangerous capability only after you've already built it and are under commercial pressure to ship. You want the pause to happen when it's cheap, when you've still got margin, rather than at the last minute when everyone's incentives are pointed the wrong way. So crossing a yellow line should be treated as a serious event — not a panic, but a real signal that the organisation needs to slow down and do the careful version of the work.

And honestly, the other piece is that we should expect to cross yellow lines. If we never trip one, that probably means the thresholds are set too high, not that the models are safe. So the response should also be institutional: have we actually built the safeguards we said we'd need? Because if a yellow line trips and the answer is "no, we haven't done the security work yet," then the policy is doing its job by forcing a pause — but it would have been much better to have done that work ahead of time.

r001.rationale: It says that if thorough evaluation finds the model does not cross the red line, Anthropic can continue and should update its yellow-line evaluations to improve their calibration.

r002.rationale: It calls for protecting the weights from theft by someone who would bypass safeguards, but does not identify resistance to non-state actors as the security standard.

r003.rationale: It calls for careful evaluation after a yellow-line trigger, but does not make release conditional on intensive red-teaming of each specific modality or capability.

astra-6.text:
I think crossing a yellow line should trigger a concrete safety response. You’re getting close to a capability where the consequences could be much more serious, so you need to understand what the model can do, strengthen the relevant safeguards, and work out what evidence would justify proceeding.

I wouldn’t treat it as automatically meaning you have to stop everything. But it also can’t just mean writing a report and carrying on as before. If you can’t establish that the safeguards are adequate, you should pause the training or deployment that would create the risk. The point of having thresholds in advance is that they actually constrain your decisions when there’s pressure to keep moving.

r001.rationale: The response calls for understanding the model’s capabilities and strengthening safeguards, but does not propose revising capability evaluations or specify that the model remains incapable of corresponding red-line dangers.

r002.rationale: The response does not identify resistance to non-state actors as the security standard.

r003.rationale: The response does not make release conditional on intensive red-teaming of each specific modality or capability.

sol-6.1.text:
I think crossing a yellow line should trigger a concrete safety process. It’s an early warning that we’re approaching capabilities where the safeguards we have today might no longer be sufficient. So we should do more intensive evaluations, work out what additional safeguards are needed, and make sure we can put those in place before crossing the corresponding red line.

I wouldn’t say that every yellow-line crossing means we should immediately stop training. But it has to change what we do. If we can’t make a credible case that we’ll have adequate safeguards in time, then we need to slow down or pause. Otherwise, the threshold isn’t doing any work.

r001.rationale: It calls for more intensive evaluations after a yellow-line crossing, but does not propose revising capability evaluations or specify the condition that the model remains incapable of the corresponding red-line dangers.

r002.rationale: It discusses safeguards generally but does not identify resistance to non-state actors as the security standard.

r003.rationale: It does not make release conditional on intensive red-teaming of each specific modality or capability.
